blocks.markdown: General contract principles still apply: one side proposes terms and the other must assent. In insurance, the details of the application, underwriting approval, policy, premium receipt, and any binding cover note or intermediary arrangement may matter in determining whether and when coverage began. Delivery of the written policy is important evidence of the agreement, but do not treat delivery alone as a universal substitute for the Insurance Code's premium rules.

**Practical checklist for a problem question.** Identify the offer/application; the insurer's acceptance or approval; the agreed subject, risk, amount, and period; whether the policy or cover note was issued/delivered; the premium and any receipt/credit/grace-period rule; and the event date compared with the effective date.

**The general rule is payment first:** a policy generally is not valid and binding until the premium is paid. The Code specifies exceptions, including a life/industrial-life grace period and a qualifying credit extension of no more than 90 days to a licensed intermediary under broker/agency agreements.

If the policy or premium receipt acknowledges payment, the acknowledgment is conclusive for making the policy binding under Section 79, even if another policy clause says it will not bind until actual payment.

Sections 64 and 66 are grouped in the syllabus under premium payment, but they deal specifically with cancellation and renewal of non-life insurance; the general statutory rule on premium payment is Section 77. Section 64 governs cancellation by the insurer of non-life insurance: nonpayment is one permissible ground but not the only one, and cancellation requires prior notice resting on a listed ground that occurred after the policy became effective. Section 65 adds that the notice must be written, identify the statutory ground, and inform the insured of the right to ask for the supporting facts.

**Trap.** Section 66 concerns non-life policy renewal, not the initial premium-payment rule. Unless proper notice is sent at least 45 days before the policy period ends, the insured is entitled to renew upon payment of the renewal premium.

An agent or broker who collects premiums must hold the money in trust and cannot keep or misuse it. When an insurer delivers the policy through an agent or broker, the Code treats that intermediary as authorized to receive the due premium on the insurer's behalf.

blocks.markdown: After three full annual premiums have been paid, the policy must describe options in case of later default: cash surrender value or paid-up insurance purchased with that value. The policy must show a year-by-year table of values and options for at least 20 years, and if the policyholder does not choose in time, one listed option automatically applies rather than all value being lost.

blocks.markdown: **Trap.** Reinstatement is not automatic merely because the insured asks for it. The policyholder must apply within three years from premium default (unless the cash surrender value was paid or the extension period expired), provide satisfactory evidence of insurability, and pay overdue premiums and policy debt with the allowed interest.

blocks.markdown: If the insurer has carried the risk and been liable for any period, even a short one, the insured generally cannot get the premium for that particular risk returned under Section 81.
**Trap.** The insured cannot use Section 82 to recover premiums where fraud is the reason the policy is rescinded or a claim denied.
